## Plasma Gasification of Medical Plastic Waste to Syngas in a Greenhouse Gas (CO2) Environment

Andrius Tamoši¯ unas 1, * , Mindaugas Milieška 1 , Dovil˙ e Gimžauskait˙ e 1 , Mindaugas Aikas 1 , Rolandas Uscila 1 , K˛ estutis Zakarauskas 2 , Sebastian Fendt 3 , Sebastian Bastek 3 and Hartmut Spliethoff 3

- 1 Plasma Processing Laboratory, Lithuanian Energy Institute, 44403 Kaunas, Lithuania; mindaugas.milieska@lei.lt (M.M.); dovile.gimzauskaite@lei.lt (D.G.); mindaugas.aikas@lei.lt (M.A.); rolandas.uscila@lei.lt (R.U.)
- 2 Laboratory of Combustion Processes, Lithuanian Energy Institute, 44403 Kaunas, Lithuania; kestutis.zakarauskas@lei.lt
- 3
- Chair of Energy Systems, Technical University of Munich, 85748 Garching, Germany; spliethoff@tum.de (H.S.)
- * Correspondence: andrius.tamosiunas@lei.lt; Tel.: +370-37-401-999

Abstract: The global coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic in early 2020 caused the amount of medical waste, especially plastic waste, to increase. The pandemic exacerbated the plastic waste management problem, including the need to find more sustainable treatment methods. This study investigated the sustainable conversion of plastic waste (FFP2-type face masks) to syngas via pure CO2 plasma gasification to recover energy and reduce environmental pollution. A direct current (DC) thermal arc plasma torch of 40.6-68.4 kW power generated the plasma stream. Carbon dioxide (CO2), as a greenhouse gas (GHG), was used as the main plasma-forming gas and gasifying agent. The 140thermal feedstock input plasma gasification system was used in the study. The effect of the CO2-to-C ratio on the gasification performance efficiency was investigated. The best CO2 plasma gasification process performance was obtained at a CO2-to-C ratio of 2.34. In these conditions, the main syngas components (H2 + CO) comprised 80.46 vol.% (H2: 24.62 vol.% and CO: 55.84 vol.%) and the following values were seen for the heating value of the syngas (LHVsyngas: 13.88 MJ/Nm 3 ), the syngas yield (3.13 Nm 3 /kgFFP2), the tar content in the syngas (23.0 g/Nm 3 ), the carbon conversion efficiency (CCE: 70.6%), and the cold gas efficiency (CGE: 47.8%). Additionally, the plasma gasification process mass and energy balance were evaluated. It was demonstrated that CO2 plasma gasification could be a promising thermochemical treatment technology for sustainable plastic waste disposal and the simultaneous utilization of greenhouse gases, such as carbon dioxide.

Keywords: sustainable waste management; FFP2 medical face mask; thermal arc plasma; greenhouse gas (CO2); syngas; mass and energy balance

## 1. Introduction

The global coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic in early 2020 caused the amount of medical waste to increase. Overall, the pandemic has increased medical waste management problems, including the need for sustainable treatment options. According to the official statistics in the United Nations Environmental Programme report, the medical waste generated by healthcare facilities as a result of COVID-19 has increased to 3.4 kg/person/day compared to the 'normal' average volume of medical hazardous waste, which ranges from 0.2 to 0.5 kg/person/day [1]. The main types of COVID-19-related medical waste include masks, gloves, gowns, antigen tests, vaccine vials and needles, and plastic packaging

and containers, with most of this waste comprising polymers (plastics, rubbers, clothing, etc.) [2,3]. Also, the public use of personal protective equipment, especially masks, has increased significantly since the pandemic. Some estimations show that in 2020, up to 3.4 billion single-use masks were discarded daily, resulting in a considerable increase in the volume of plastic waste [4,5]. However, after the suppression of the first global wave of COVID-19, the use of protective masks in public (but not in the healthcare sector) has sharply decreased. Nevertheless, problems surrounding sustainable waste management, especially of plastic waste, and environmental pollution still exist. The World Health Organization (WHO), in its 2020 report, states that three out of ten healthcare facilities lack medical waste segregation systems. Also, fewer than one in three healthcare facilities in the least developed countries have a basic waste management service [6,7]. The healthcare sector makes a substantial contribution to greenhouse gas emissions, accounting for approx. 4-5% of total emissions [8,9]. Thus, COVID-19-related issues, including post-COVID-19, have made medical waste generation a global challenge [10].

Current medical waste management practice is based on the 3Rs (reduce, reuse, and recycle) concept. However, further treatment and disposal of medical waste is unavoidable to manage it safely and rationally. The three main options for treating medical waste are chemical treatment, autoclaving, and incineration, which are further divided into subcategories [11,12]. The residual waste remaining after any of the treatment options mentioned above is mainly disposed of in landfills. In this regard, more advanced medical waste treatment methods have been investigated over the years. Besides the use of medical waste incineration to produce power and heat, conventional thermochemical methods, such as pyrolysis and gasification, enable the conversion of waste to higher-added-value products, for instance, syngas, bio-oil, and biochar. Catalysts are usually utilized to overcome any issues with the final product quality improvement, energy consumption, and process cost reduction [13,14]. However, this causes additional problems, requiring catalyst recovery due to the deactivation of the catalyst by unavoidable side product streams such as tars, the need for expensive additional gas cleaning systems, or special waste pre-treatment requirements.

Plasma gasification for waste treatment has been considered as an advanced and more sustainable treatment method that enables, due to the very high temperatures (2000-5000 ◦ C), the conversion of (hazardous) waste to gaseous compounds and vitrified solid inert slag [15-17]. Plasma offers a unique charged particle medium, such as electrons, ions, radicals, etc., which accelerates the conversion reaction kinetics and chemistry much faster than conventional gasification methods. It has been applied to several waste feedstock conversions, such as biomass, municipal solid waste (MSW), refuse-derived fuels (RDF), sewage sludge, medical waste, and plastic waste [17-23]. Various gases and their mixtures, for instance, air, nitrogen, argon, steam, carbon dioxide, etc., can be used to form plasma. Corresponding to global warming, direct carbon dioxide utilization via the carbon capture and utilization (CCU) process could be one of the solutions, as carbon dioxide can be used simultaneously as the gasifying agent, the main plasma gas, and the heat carrier, thus contributing to lowering emissions [24-27].

In this regard, to contribute to solving waste management problems, this experimental study aimed to investigate the possibility of gasifying medical plastic waste, i.e., FFP2-type face masks, to syngas by DC thermal arc plasma technology using carbon dioxide as the plasma-forming gas, the heat carrier, and the reactant. The performance of the plasma gasification system was quantified based on key process parameters, such as the producer gas composition and quality, the carbon conversion efficiency, the cold gas efficiency, and the specific energy requirement. Additionally, the process mass and energy balance were evaluated.

## 2. Materials and Methods

## 2.1. Plastic Feedstock Characterization, Pre-Treatment, and Dosing

The FFP2 face mask comprises four layers of fabric, with polypropylene (PP) and polyethylene (PE) used as the basic materials for the filter layers. Table 1 describes the proximate and ultimate analysis of the FFP2 face mask material used as a feedstock for the thermal plasma gasification to syngas.

The FFP2 fabric was shredded to pieces and later granulated to pellets measuring 8.0 ± 0.5 mm in diameter (one pellet weighed around 0.5 ± 0.005 g). This pre-treatment step ensured a stabilized dosage of the feedstock from a 70 l hopper via a screw feeder to the reactor, regulated by a frequency converter. The reactor's average constant feeding rate of FFP2 granules was around 10.58 kg/h. Before the experiments, the pellet dosing was calibrated by checking the average mass flow rate, as the screw feeder, in general, cannot provide very smooth continuous dosing. Additionally, the mean mass flow rate of the FFP2 pellets fed to the plasma gasifier per measured unit time was checked after the experiments by weighing the remaining feedstock in the hopper. The difference from the initial tests was below 8%.

## 2.2. Plasma Gasifier

The experimental plasma gasification system, shown in Figure 1, was designed and built at the Plasma Processing Laboratory of the Lithuanian Energy Institute. The 140 kWth input plasma gasifier with a reactor length of 1.3 m and an inner diameter of 0.2 m (reactor volume 0.04 m 3 ) was used to carry out the experiments. The inner reactor walls were insulated with a 25 mm thick ceramic material made of aluminum oxide.

The main parts of the system consist of the following: 1-an atmospheric pressure DC arc plasma torch, 2-a feedstock hopper with a screw feeder, 3-a cyclone, 4-a gas quencher, 5-a gas burner, 6-a rotameter, 7-a gas and tar sampling port, 8-a condensate removal system, 9-a plasma-chemical reactor, 10-an ash/char hopper, 11-a power supply, 12-a plasma-forming and -shielding gas supply, 13-a plasma torch cooling system, and T1, T2, T3, T4, T5, T6, T7-thermocouples.

The DC thermal arc plasma torch, installed at the bottom of the reactor, of 40.6-68.4 kW power (I = 160-190 A, U = 250-380 V, η = 0.58-0.73) operating at atmospheric pressure served as a device to heat the carbon dioxide (CO2) to an average temperature of 3250-3650 ± 50 K. Carbon dioxide, known as a GHG, was simultaneously used as the plasma-forming gas, the heat carrier, and the reactant. No other gas was used to form the plasma. The mass flow rate of the CO2 was in the range of 11.56-21.13 kg/h. The FFP2 pellets dropped from the top of the reactor came into direct contact with a high-temperature CO2 plasma stream on a moving grate, where it was converted to gaseous products. Below the moving grate was a bunker for the unconverted solid char/ash collection.

Thermal CO2 splitting is a highly endothermic reaction. However, at temperatures between 3000 K and 3500 K, thermal CO2 splitting is thermodynamically and energetically favorable because of the higher-equilibrium CO2 conversion of 45-80% and the lower reaction enthalpy of 206 kJ/mol [32]. In this temperature range, the theoretical energy efficiency is around 47%, which goes down to 35% at 5000 K, even if the CO2 conversion reaches 100% [33]. Due to some technical limitations in heating the reactor and avoiding It can be seen that during the gasifier preheating step (until 10:29:30), the CO2 concentration decreased from 74% to around 60% and the CO concentration increased to 23% due to the CO2-splitting reaction (R1). This means that one of the syngas constituents, carbon monoxide, was formed during the thermal CO2 decomposition by the electric arc of the plasma torch. Due to some technical limitations in heating the reactor and avoiding the melting of the grate, the reactor was not in an entirely steady state, reaching the maximum COconcentrations after the CO2 splitting. However, it was close to a steady-state condition, as observed during several experiments. After making some reactor modifications, this phenomenon will be thoroughly examined to investigate the highest possible CO concentration and compare it with the theoretical CO2 conversion and energy efficiency. After the gasifier's preheating step with CO production via CO2 splitting, the plasma gasification of the FFP2 pellets took over. In this case, gasification reactions occurred, enhancing the CO production to a total volumetric concentration of around 53-56% and further reducing the CO2 to 6-8%. Thus, the CO production was affected by two dominant processes, i.e., the CO2 splitting and the major chemical gasification reactions between the CO2/CO plasma stream and the FFP2 feedstock (thermal cracking, Boudouard, partial oxidation, and other chemical reactions) [26,32,34].

## 3.2. Effect of the CO2 -to-Carbon (CO2-to-C) Ratio on the Gasification Process Performance

During the plasma gasification step of the conversion of the FFP2 pellets to syngas, the effect of the CO2 to carbon present in the feedstock (CO2-to-C ratio) was investigated. As the mass flow of the FFP2 was kept constant at 10.58 kg/h, the carbon content did not

change over time. The main varying parameter was the mass flow of the CO2 (the only gasifying medium and plasma-forming gas), which was in the 11.56-21.13 kg/h range. It should be noted that changing the mass flow of the CO2 also affected the power of the plasma torch due to a voltage drop in the electric arc discharge chamber. Thus, by increasing the CO2 flow rate from 11.56 to 21.13 kg/h, the plasma torch power increased from 40.6 to 68.4 kW and more energy was transferred to the reactor.

As the CO2-to-C ratio increased from 1.26 to 2.34, the volumetric concentrations of the gaseous components in the producer gas changed, as shown in Figure 3. The major gas component was CO (52.86-55.84 vol.%), followed by H2 (20.61-24.62 vol.%), CO2 (6.55-8.24 vol.%), CH4 (5.83-7.64 vol.%), C2H2 (~3 vol.%), and traces of other light C2-C3 hydrocarbons. The reason for the increasing CO concentration may be the dominance of the CO2-splitting (R1) and Boudouard reactions (R2), while the production of H2 can be explained by the feedstock thermal cracking (R3) and the water-gas shift reactions (R4). Thermal plasma provides a high-temperature region for partial oxidation, cracking, reforming, and other reactions when directly contacting the plastic pellets at short residence times. Therefore, the cracking process at high temperatures resulted in higher volumes of gaseous products, such as H2, and less coke formation [35,36]. There were also several reactions involving methane formation: (R5), (R6), and (R7). Syngas (H2 + CO) generally constituted more than 76.08-80.46 vol.% in the producer gas.

The higher CO concentration in this study could be due to the pure CO2 used as the primary plasma gas, which had a longer residence time when passing and contacting the electric arc of the plasma torch and thus splitting into CO and O2. Besides, instead of pure CO2, a mixture of CO2 + O2 + Ar as the gasifying medium and plasma gas was reported in [18]. Mallick and Vairakannu and Li et al. [25,26,37] reported using pure CO2 plasma gasification of the selected feedstock in the 1.12-2.0 kW plasma torch power range. The CO concentration was around 52% in the computer keyboard plastic waste conversion case, but not at the optimal process conditions. Sikarwar et al. [38] also reported a similar CO concentration of around 57 vol.%. However, CO2 was used only as the gasifying agent, whereas Ar + H2O was used as the plasma-forming gas, yielding a higher H2 content. In general, the difference in the design of the plasma torch and its power may affect the residence time splitting of the CO2, and thus the CO concentration may differ. Also, different feedstocks may influence the CO concentration due to their different compositions and process conditions, i.e., the dominance of the Boudouard (R2) and partial oxidation reactions. In some cases, the content of other syngas compounds in the present study, such as H2, is similar to (RDF [18] and electrical switch waste [26]) or lower than (RDF [25] and keyboard plastic waste [37]) the results reported in the literature. This was mainly attributed to the different process conditions, such as the extra gasifying agents (H2O, O2, etc.) used and the feedstock elemental composition, affecting the dominant chemical reactions.

The change in the CO2-to-C ratio had no significant effect on the lower heating value of the syngas (LHVsyngas). As the CO2-to-C ratio increased from 1.26 to 2.34, the LHVsyngas remained stable in the range of 13.5-13.88 MJ/Nm 3 , as shown in Figure 4. This was also the case for the H2/CO ratio, which was in the range of 0.38-0.44. The LHVsyngas obtained in this research was higher compared to the CO2 plasma gasification of RDF and bakelitebased plastic waste and equal to the pure CO2 plasma gasification of RDF [18,26,38]. The pure CO2 plasma gasification of the computer keyboard plastic waste in the DC arc plasma of 2 kW power yielded a higher syngas calorific value of 16.46 MJ/Nm 3 [37]. However, the authors reported that the operating conditions were not optimum for this process case. At the best process performance (P = 1.12 kW, 0.5 lpm of CO2, and 40 g/10 min of feedstock mass flow rate), the LHVsyngas was 15.8 MJ/Nm 3 . , x FOR PEER REVIEW 8  of  15 the best process performance (P = 1.12 kW, 0.5 lpm of CO2, and 40 g/10 min of feedstock mass fl ow rate), the LHVsyngas was 15.8 MJ/Nm 3 .

Additionally, the tar content obtained in the syngas was relatively high and ranged from 23 to 32.9 g/Nm 3 . The higher the CO2-to-C ratio, the lower the tar concentration determined. This could be explained by the higher plasma torch power transferred to the reactor while converting the feedstock, which increased by around 40%, i.e., from 40.6 to 68.4 kW. The increased plasma torch power was mainly affected by the increased mass flow rate of the CO2 used as a plasma-forming gas. Thus, with the electric arc current kept constant, the increased plasma-forming gas flow rate affected the increase of the arc's voltage drop. As a result, the plasma torch power increased. The most abundant tar compounds were benzene (12.6-16.75 g/Nm 3 ), toluene (1.69-5.0 g/Nm 3 ), and naphthalene (3.0-3.75 g/Nm 3 ), altogether comprising more than 75-77% of the total tar composition. However, the obtained tar content was high and would require further syngas processing and upgrading. The reason for the higher tar concentration was that the generated plasma itself was the only heat source heating the whole reactor. No other additional electric heating of the reactor walls was used in the process, which would have increased the energy penalty and ultimately lowered the CGE. Thus, the design of the plasma gasifier could affect the final desirable gaseous product but could be improved by installing a low-power additional plasma torch (up to a few kilowatts) or catalytic cleaning. In general, plasma gasification is a method for high-purity syngas production with extremely low tar content [39]; however, it requires balancing the process performance and the energy efficiency. For instance, Hlina et al. reported a tar content of 10 mg/Nm 3 after wood biomass argon/water vapor plasma gasification. Agon et al. [40] used the same plasma gasifier as the previous researcher cited, but this time for RDF plasma gasification using different gasifying agents (CO2 + O2, H2O, CO2 + H2O, and O2 + H2O). In this case, the total tar content in the syngas was in the range of 0.132-0.543 g/Nm 3 , with the most abundant tar compounds being naphthalene, acenaphthylene, and phenanthrene [18]. The plasma gasifier was electrically preheated for 24 h to 1200 K to prevent the destruction of the ceramic coating in all the reported cases. In this research, the reactor was not externally preheated; all of the heat came from the plasma torch.

The dependence of the CO2-to-C ratio on the syngas yield, as well as the H2 and CO yield, is shown in Figure 5. As the CO2-to-C ratio increased from 1.26 to 2.34, the syngas yield produced from 1 kg of FFP2 plastic feedstock increased from 1.77 Nm 3 to 3.13 Nm 3 . This was mainly attributed to the increased mass flow rate of the CO2 used as the plasma gas and the gasifying medium, thus increasing the CO content and yield in the producer gas due to the CO2-splitting (R1) and Boudouard (R2) reactions. The H2 yield constantly increased, possibly due to the water-gas shift (R3) and thermal feedstock cracking reactions. The obtained syngas yield corresponds well with the CO2 plasma gasification of RDF, as reported by [38]. The authors claim the highest producer gas yield of 3.44 Nm 3 /kgRDF at the RDF feeding rate of 11.3 kg/h. The higher syngas yields could be a reason for the higher carbon-to-gas conversion rate, which the authors mentioned above also reported. The highest yields of the separate syngas compounds, H2 and CO, were obtained at a CO2-to-C ratio of 2.34, reaching their highest values of 43.24% and 68.59%, respectively. Agon et al. [18] reported a similar CO yield of 67% using a CO2 + O2 mixture as a gasifying agent (cases 1, 2). However, the reported H2 yield of 76% was around 43% higher than in the present study. This could be due to the DC water/argon plasma torch used in their research, where water was the main plasma-forming gas, but a CO2 + O2 gas mixture was added as the main gasifying agent. Thus, some of the H2 could have come from the water-splitting reaction by the electric arc.

The e ff ect of the CO2-to-C ratio on the carbon conversion e ffi ciency (CCE) and cold gas e ffi ciency (CGE) is shown in Figure 6. As the CO2-to-C ratio increased from 1.26 to 2.34, the CCE and the CGE increased from 41.1% and 30.57% to 70.6% and 47.8%, respectively. The CCE increase was mainly a ff ected by the increase in the plasma torch power from 40.6 kW to 68.4 kW, meaning that more energy was transferred directly from the plasma stream to the FFP2 feedstock to be gasi fi ed. The increased mass fl ow rate of the CO2  used  as  the  plasma  gas  and  gasifying  medium  a ff ected  the  higher  plasma  torch power. This in fl uenced the increase in the voltage drop of the plasma torch electric circuit without the need to increase the current, which would have led to a decrease in the coeffi cient of thermal e ffi ciency. As a result, the plasma stream transferred more power at a higher e ffi ciency to the reactor with lower losses to the plasma torch cooling water. Higher CCE values were reported by Agon et al. [18] and Sikarwar et al. [38] gasifying RDF: 83% and 100%, respectively. It could be that the plasma torch power was much higher in the referenced cases, exceeding 90-120 kW, and that the reactor was preheated before the experiments, and thus more energy was transferred to the reactor, and/or there were some methodological di ff erences. As the CO2-to-C ratio increased from 1.26 to 2.34, the CCE and the CGE increased from 41.1% and 30.57% to 70.6% and 47.8%, respectively. The CCE increase was mainly affected by the increase in the plasma torch power from 40.6 kW to 68.4 kW, meaning that more energy was transferred directly from the plasma stream to the FFP2 feedstock to be gasified. The increased mass flow rate of the CO2 used as the plasma gas and gasifying medium affected the higher plasma torch power. This influenced the increase in the voltage drop of the plasma torch electric circuit without the need to increase the current, which would have led to a decrease in the coefficient of thermal efficiency. As a result, the plasma stream transferred more power at a higher efficiency to the reactor with lower losses to the plasma torch cooling water. Higher CCE values were reported by Agon et al. [18] and Sikarwar et al. [38] gasifying RDF: 83% and 100%, respectively. It could be that the plasma torch power was much higher in the referenced cases, exceeding 90-120 kW, and that the reactor was preheated before the experiments, and thus more energy was transferred to the reactor, and/or there were some methodological differences. In our case, for precision, not only was the amount of carbon present in the FFP2 feedstock and from the CO2 as tthe gasifying agent taken into consideration, but the amount of carbon that remained in the ash/char and tar was also evaluated.

Bycomparing the CGEs, it can be determined that, in our case, the value of 47.8% is higher than that reported in other referenced plasma gasification cases using CO2 or its mixtures as gasifying agents for RDF and plastic waste conversion [18,25,26,37,38]. However, the difference is insignificant, reaching CGE values of up to 46%. In one case, Li et al. [26] reported that the highest obtained CGE value was 49.9% during CO2 plasma gasification of RDF. Despite this, the process conditions were not optimal. At the optimal conditions, the CGE was only 39.6%. Generally, CGE in lab-scale plasma gasification is not an optimized performance parameter compared to the industrial process, where the process heat would have been recovered and reused. However, the CGE of plasma gasification is still lower than that of conventional gasification, where the CGE is usually in the range of 60-80%. This is because plasma needs electricity to run the allothermal gasification process. Thus, to increase the CGE in plasma gasification, wastes/feedstocks with a higher calorific value should be used. Also, the process should be performed at the lowest possible plasma torch power so as not to ruin the CCE. Even the CGE of plasma gasification is lower compared to conventional gasification, but the plasma method's versatility compensates for this in

An integrated medical waste-to-energy concept was numerically investigated, coupling plasma Figure 7 shows the Sankey diagram of the mass balance of the FFP2 pellets' CO2 plasma gasification to syngas at the highest CO2-to-C ratio of 2.34. At this ratio, the highest plasma gasification process efficiency was achieved. The ultimate desired product, syngas, comprised more than 92.0% of the final mass composition. Almost 8.0% of the final product composition was associated with losses forming by-products. The main by-product constituent was solid char/ash, which comprised around 74.5% of the total by-product mass, followed by tars (17.1%) and condensate (8.3%). In general, the plasma reduced solid residues to less than 18 wt% of the primary input FFP2 feedstock material. As described above, the tar content could be reduced by installing an extra-small-power plasma torch to thermally crack the heavy hydrocarbons into lighter ones. Other methods, such as physical treatment or catalytic reforming, could also be considered [43].

The Sankey energy fl ow diagram of gasifying the FFP2 plastic pellets in the CO2 thermal plasma environment was de fi ned at the same CO2-to-C ratio of 2.34 as for the mass balance case and is shown in Figure 8. The highest energy content of 69.15% after the plasma gasi fi cation was obtained in the syngas, followed by the energy loss due to radiation and reactor cooling by air (21.3%), and further energy was stored in the ash/char (7.2%), tars (2.2%), and condensate (0.047%). The option of further syngas utilization after the conditioning step is theoretically proposed for use in the gas microturbine and/or internal combustion engine (ICE). As the syngas-to-electricity conversion e ffi ciency in the microturbine is higher due to the microturbine's higher conversion performance e ffi ciency (20% compared to the ICE e ffi ciency of 17%), the la tt er case option is shown in Figure 8 [44]. Around 36% (or 24.48 kWh) of the electrical energy could be recovered to power the plasma torch (this was lower for the ICE case, at 30.4% or 20.8 kWh). The remaining energy could be recovered as heat stored in hot water. The overall process e ffi ciency of converting the syngas to electricity via the microturbine was 12.7%, and was slightly lower for the ICE at 10.8%. For comparison, Karellas et al. [45] reported a 12-18% e ffi ciency in electricity production by coupling biomass gasi fi cation with a Capstone C30 turbine with an electrical e ffi ciency of 26% and a power output of 30 kW. ## thermal plasma at a CO2-to-C ratio of 2.34. 4. Conclusions

The optional method of converting syngas to fuels via the Fischer-Tropsch process was not considered, as the H2/CO ratio would require a signi fi cant syngas upgrade via the additional water-gas shift process to reach the optimal ratio 2. This method would be more bene fi cial if water vapor were used as a gasifying agent, yielding a higher H2 concentration in the syngas. 4. Conclusions This experimental work investigated the plasma gasi fi cation of FFP2 respirator face masks to syngas in a greenhouse gas (CO2) environment to reduce the environmental polThis experimental work investigated the plasma gasification of FFP2 respirator face masks to syngas in a greenhouse gas (CO2) environment to reduce the environmental pollution caused by plastic waste and anthropogenic CO2 emissions and simultaneously to recover energy. A DC thermal arc plasma torch operating at atmospheric pressure generated a plasma stream for allothermal gasification. The effect of the CO2-to-C ratio on the gasification performance efficiency was analyzed. The highest CO2 plasma gasification efficiency was obtained at the highest CO2-to-C ratio of 2.34. At these conditions, the main syngas components (H2 + CO) comprised 80.46 vol.% (H2: 24.62 vol.% and CO: 55.84 vol.%), the LHVsyngas was 13.88 MJ/Nm 3 , the syngas yield was 3.13 Nm 3 /kgFFP2, the tar content in the syngas was 23 g/Nm 3 , the CCE was 70.6%, and the CGE was 47.8%. Additionally, the plasma gasification process mass and energy balance were analyzed.

At these conditions, the main The results show that CO2 plasma gasification is a promising thermochemical treatment method for more sustainable plastic waste conversion and the utilization of greenhouse gases, such as carbon dioxide. Future work will investigate CO2 splitting to CO using this system and maximize the gasification performance to determine the optimal process parameters.
